example_text:
**Pregnancy and Delivery: Caleb Whitfield’s mother was 28 years old at delivery. She received regular prenatal care and Caleb Whitfield was born at 41+ weeks, weighing 8 pounds 13 ounces and measuring 22.5 inches. During pregnancy, the mother experienced a sub chorionic hematoma, used Sudafed and Allegra for allergies, and had one round of antibiotics for a respiratory infection. She also received the H1N1 vaccination, which caused adverse reactions. Caleb Whitfield was delivered vaginally, with skin-to-skin contact after birth. He was sluggish about breastfeeding due to Nubaim administered during labor and required monitoring for low blood sugar and sluggish feeding for two nights post-birth. Due to the low blood sugar, circumcision was delayed several weeks. That procedure was traumatic with healing challenges due to the wound re-adhering.**

**Childhood Development: Caleb Whitfield was breastfed until about age 3 and had no significant feeding difficulties. He achieved developmental milestones such as crawling at 9 months, sitting alone at 5.5 months, standing alone at 9-10 months, and walking before 12 months. He said his first word at 10.5 months and was stringing words together by 12 months. He was fully toilet trained somewhat late, by 4.5 years.**

Caleb Whitfield has had minimal hospitalizations, including an ambulance ride for a croup attack which was traumatic for Caleb Whitfield.  He more recently had an overnight stay in the Emergency Department for apparent dehydration. He was very shaky and couldn’t get warm after a day at the water park last summer. He hadn’t eaten much that day. In the ED, they gave him IV fluids and ran EKG. Caleb Whitfield recovered and was released a few hours later, but vomited all over the ground on the way out, a fairly common reaction to the IV fluids.

**Current Health: Caleb Whitfield is 5 feet 7 inches tall and weighs 150 pounds. His healthcare provider is Dr. Patrick Reyes, and his last routine check-up was in the spring of 2024. His hearing was last evaluated several years ago with no concerns. His eye care provider is Dr. Osei at Clearview Optometric, Rocklin, and his last visit was in September 2023, with results better than 20/20. Caleb Whitfield’s dentist is Dr. Naidu at Family Smiles Dentistry, with his last visit in September 2024, resulting in a successful filling following a routine cleaning.**

Caleb Whitfield has no current health concerns and a major shift towards health occurred at age 8-9 years. In his first 7 years, Caleb Whitfield had croup chronically, persistent eczema, strep throat, and ear infections. He was diagnosed at age 5 following a strep infection with Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections (PANDAS). Illness had led to significant behavioral shifts, including mood swings and compulsive behaviors. Extensive bloodwork in 2017 revealed high strep antibodies despite no symptoms of illness, confirming the diagnosis. Caleb Whitfield underwent long-term antibiotic treatment for about four months, followed by homeopathic remedies, which proved most effective in managing his symptoms. Caleb Whitfield’s sleep patterns were a major problem until about age ten. Caleb Whitfield previously experienced night terrors, night waking and very early morning wakings. He has a big appetite, particularly for carbs, and the family maintains a gluten and dairy-free household. To maintain blood sugar, Caleb Whitfield has to eat regularly. Mood shifts often cue a need for food.

Caleb Whitfield is followed by a Dr. Patrick Reyes who specializes in Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, Osteopathic Medicine, Pain Medicine and Public Health & General Preventive Medicine whom he sees regularly. He also sees Dr. Aaron Whitfield for psychiatric care. He takes several medications for diagnosed ADHD, symptoms of mood disorder, and anxiety including 100 mg Strattera for ADHD, 150 mg Zoloft for anxiety, 300 mg Trileptal for sound sensitivity, 25 mg Topomax (reportedly discontinuing soon but was on board to try and balance blood sugar and mood), 1 mg low dose naltrexone (LDN) for inflammation, Vitamin D3+K2 for immune support, and 300 mg Seroquel for sleep and mood swings. Previous medications included Dyanavel, Intuniv, and Geodon, which were discontinued due to various side effects such as motor tics, undesirable mood and/or behavior changes,  weight gain, negative thoughts, self harm,  and efficacy issues.  These experiences highlight the importance of carefully considering Caleb Whitfield's medication history to avoid reintroducing treatments that have previously been ineffective or detrimental.

example_text:
**SCHOOL HISTORY**

Complete cumulative school records were viewed by this evaluator and are summarized as follows:

Diego Fenton was a student in the Fairview City School District from  kindergarten through 8th grades where he attended Green Oaks Elementary and Hartwell Middle School. Attendance was consistently good. In kindergarten and first grades he was noted to need to work on handwriting but met all other expectations. Diego Fenton received additional small group writing instruction for handwriting (letter formation and spacing) in first grade and for punctuation and handwriting in second grade. Behaviorally, Diego Fenton was noted to be socially enthusiastic about learning, but needed improvement in staying on task, following rules and focusing on precision and accuracy. He was at grade level in all areas except writing, which was slightly below. Diego Fenton met standards in third grade but continued to demonstrate attention difficulties. In fourth grade during the first trimester, in Language Arts, Diego Fenton was noted to “exhibit poor listening skills by engaging in side conversations.” There were no other concerns noted through fifth grades and all areas socially, behaviorally, and academically were rated at the proficient or basic levels.

The COVID-19 Pandemic caused schools to move to distance learning during the third semester of seventh grade. Prior to lock-down, during the first two semesters, Diego Fenton did well meeting standards in World Languages, Physical Education, Speaking and Listening and Reading, but he was below grade level expectations in all other areas. Learning behaviors including work completion and utilizing feedback and resources were problematic in Language Arts and Social Studies, but more consistent in all other classes. During Distance Learning, the Physical Education teacher noted that “Interventions were provided, including sit administrator and psychologist/counselor, but the student rarely participated in DL.” Diego Fenton passed all of his classes in 8th grade but demonstrated inconsistent work completion and engagement.

Diego Fenton holds a 1.41 total GPA at Meadowbrook High School where he enrolled in August 2021 as a freshman. Diego Fenton has attempted 155 credits and passed 125. He needs 135 more credits to graduate. Diego Fenton did well his first semester of freshman year, earning a 2.75 grade point average. By second semester, his GPA went down to 1.50 and included significant discipline infractions included fighting, being out of class without permission, walking around in the wetlands behind campus during school, and being disrespectful towards staff. Diego Fenton reported this was when he began using drugs and alcohol. Last year as a sophomore, Diego Fenton had a total of seven absences, 39 periods tardy, 34 period truancies and ten days suspension. Suspensions were due to profanity, possession of drug paraphernalia/ vaping products, and possession of a controlled substance on school grounds.  This semester grades at first progress check were Positive Power- A, Weight Conditioning- A+, CCIM1- B and  US History- C with the comment, “Showing Improvement.”

The report completed by Meadowbrook High School indicated that In September of 2022, Diego Fenton was diagnosed as having Bi-Polar Disorder with Psychosis, ADHD-Combined Type, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder by Family Nurse Practitioner, Tanya Brooks, before she knew he was abusing drugs. In October 2022, Dr. Manning diagnosed Diego Fenton with Opioid Use Disorder, due to an addiction to Fentanyl. Adriana Fenton reportedly requested a 504 meeting to address the diagnoses and the possibility of implementing a Behavior Intervention Plan. After Diego Fenton was again suspended due to possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia/vaping products, parents signed an assessment plan. A 504 Accommodation plan for these diagnoses was put in place in December 2022 with the following accommodations:

1.     Diego Fenton is allowed to take a maximum of one short break per period to the wellness center when showing signs of inattention or frustration. Usually seen by bouncing his leg or being very fidgety. Student will use a card on his desk as a non-verbal que that he needs a break.

2.     Preferential seating near teacher’s primary area of instruction.

3.     Non-verbal and/or subtle redirection when off-task.

During student observations in two classes by the examiner, the above listed accommodations were implemented, with the exception of #1, which was not needed.

example_text:
**PREVIOUS ASSESSMENT**

Mason Kessler underwent a Multidisciplinary Psycho-educational Evaluation in fourth grade at NCSA. Score summaries are located in Addendum 2 at the end of this report. This assessment indicated Mason Kessler had above average cognitive ability with no areas of processing weakness, including auditory, visual, sensory motor, verbal, attention and reasoning. While sensory motor processing fell within the average range, a poor pencil grip was noted to impact speed of writing. Observations of executive functioning identified a broad level of concerns, but Mason Kessler was accessing his education and making growth.  He demonstrated average to well above average academic skills. Mason Kessler had friends and his non-verbal as well as pragmatic language skills fell within the average range. A 504 Plan was developed as educational need could not be identified.

example_text:
**Parent Input**

Mrs. Palmer provided the following input:

Sydney Palmer lives at home with her parents and older brother. Her medical history is significant for being induced prematurely and weighing four and a half pounds at birth. Sydney Palmer spent a week in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, including time in an incubator. She was treated for a tongue tie with a frenulum clip. Sydney Palmer is currently receiving medical care and treatment for anxiety (Social and OCD) and depression and there is also a family history of anxiety and depression. Sydney Palmer takes Zoloft with no reported side effects. No significant family stressors, trauma, illnesses or accidents are reported. Sydney Palmer does have sensory sensitivities which impact her eating. Sydney Palmer’s diet and sleep are reported as relatively normal at this time. In regards to symptoms of depression, Sydney Palmer has good days and bad days. She has become very sedentary the past few years

Developmental milestones were on time except for talking which was delayed until after age three. Sydney Palmer had early intervention through Sierra Vista Regional Center and attended a language immersive preschool through her school district from ages three to four. She always struggled with math and qualified for an IEP in second grade.

When asked if there was any specific social trauma, Mrs. Palmer indicates that she does not think there was any one event and Sydney Palmer was okay when she initially came back to school from Covid-19 closures in 7th grade in a hybrid model from March to end of May that year. Sydney Palmer got close with one friend, but when all students returned to campus in 8th grade, that friend went back to her previous crowd, and that was really devastating for Sydney Palmer. As the 8th grade year went on, her social circle got smaller and smaller by her own choice, I think as a way to avoid getting hurt again and possibly to avoid difficult goodbyes, as she would not be going to the same high school as her peers. This was also by her own choice; Sydney Palmer was at a charter in Sacramento and wanted to go to the neighborhood school her brothers had attended for high school). By the end of eighth grade, she didn't have any friends, but was looking forward to a fresh start in high school.

In the first week or so of summer between freshman and sophomore year, Sydney Palmer got sick with a stomach bug while her dad and I were out of town. She had already been suffering with anxiety and OCD, and an extreme fear of throwing up. That event, perhaps more than anything, let to a steep decline in her mental health. She was treated for avoidant restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) as a result, and stopped wanting to get in the car, for fear of getting carsick. She was in a very bad place, mentally, when freshman year started, and that is when the family really saw the effects of the social anxiety. Sydney Palmer had to take a leave from school (she did independent study) from late September through the beginning of January to do outpatient treatment at the Anxiety Treatment Center. When she returned to school in January, her social anxiety was as present as it had been before, although she was functioning slightly better in other ways. Sydney Palmer has been seeing this therapist for a year, was with another one for the year prior to that (that therapist moved), and before that, had a therapist with Kaiser.

Mother indicates that her concerns, “have been that the school (the math teachers in particular, but also the IEP team) did not provide Sydney Palmer with a free and appropriate education in Integrated Math 2. She was not given appropriate accommodations, and the only help they offered was given outside the regular class time. We paid for private tutoring one or two times per weekly depending on whether there was a test. Sydney Palmer turned in almost all of her homework and class assignments, earning A in those areas, but she failed quizzes and tests.  The onus was 100% on Sydney Palmer to pass the class, without sensitivity or consideration of her learning disability. The teachers were inflexible and admitted to not having experience in dyscalculia. Even the Education Specialist in her co-taught class did not take any responsibility for making the material more accessible for her. Sydney Palmer received an F for the first half of the course, which she made up before school with a general education teacher in the math department to a D- (that was part of an agreement that once Sydney Palmer hit a D, they would be finished). Sydney Palmer had to do this make-up while learning the material for the second half of the course simultaneously, which was just not feasible for her. She got an F for the second half as well. We pleaded for better accommodations or a modification to the weighting of the grading (it was something like 85% on tests, 10% quizzes, and 5% homework). We were told “no” over and over again by the IEP team. Mrs. Palmer states that, “The school told us the only way they would consider looking at making changes was if they did a brand new assessment, even though her triennial wasn't due until next year. We agreed (on the advice of our attorney), and what came out of that was that she no longer qualified as having a learning disability in math, and that it was her "emotional disturbance" that was causing her to perform so poorly in math. That led to the IEE request.”

**Therapist Input**

Rachel Simmons is Sydney Palmer’s private therapist. She provided the following input:

1.      Challenges: What do you perceive as Sydney Palmer's most significant challenges in the school environment?

     “In my work with Sydney Palmer as her individual therapist, she and I have identified her social anxiety and OCD to be her biggest challenges at school. Some of her symptomatic expressions of social anxiety include distress in asking for support from or approaching teachers; she reports she will often not ask for help for fear of being perceived as dumb, or even to prevent feeling all eyes on her/being noticed by peers. Additionally, her OCD can create obstacles to her attendance to instruction in class if she has a compulsion to erase entire class notes due to one mistake, and then be unable to recreate the information nor attend to the current information being supplied.” 

2.      **Effective Strategies:** _Are there any strategies or support systems currently in place that you feel are working particularly well for her?_

   “Ashely’s biggest support system comes from her parents, particularly her mom with whom she is very comfortable relating her struggles and asking for advice from. Sydney Palmer has not specifically identified interventions at school that have worked particularly well (though that may be due to our session focus being elsewhere).”

3.      **Impact of Math Difficulties:** _How has her lack of success in math class affected her overall well-being and school experience?_

    “Sydney Palmer struggles with self-esteem and her perception that others are thinking negatively about her. Her struggles in math compound the feelings of low self-worth, which impact other areas of school experiences. She reports little confidence with being able to become successful in math.”

4.      Diagnoses and Recommendations: Based on your sessions with Sydney Palmer, do you have any diagnoses or recommendations that could inform the school’s approach to her education?

  “Sydney Palmer's Social Anxiety and OCD diagnoses seem to be impacting her school experiences and performance the most. Interventions with those in mind may be more successful. It is often that she may be limiting herself from asking for help from teachers or peers due to her Social Anxiety, particularly anxiety around how they may perceive her or if she's feeling especially anxious about having any attention paid to her. Sydney Palmer's OCD symptoms are primarily covert - the struggle is often invisible driven by obsessive thoughts and compulsions usually showing up as a 'need' to abort or avoid the task at hand, or perform a compulsion that impacts her ability to keep up (as in the need to erase the entirety of class notes to rectify one mistake). When she is experiencing OCD symptoms, her attention is greatly reduced elsewhere.  Sydney Palmer has great desire to do well in school, both for her future and for her families' and her own expectations. She is very frustrated by the anxiety and OCD symptoms that can often impair her in being as successful as she wants to be.”

5.      School's Role: In your view, how can the school further assist Sydney Palmer in her learning journey, especially in addressing her math-related challenges?

    “Exploration of any anxieties/intrusive thoughts that she may be experiencing, and the compulsions that may be associated with them could aid the interventionist's understanding of the role her diagnoses may or may not be playing in that particular learning experience.”
    
    **Education Pathways** **Teacher Input**

Education Pathways teacher, Melisa Whitcombe, provided the following input of Sydney Palmer's performance and behavior in her class.

## Work Habits and Behavior

Sydney Palmer is described as a diligent student who initiates work independently, scoring an 'Above Average' rating in this area. She is persistent in her efforts and does not give up easily. While her concentration and attentiveness are rated as 'Average,' she is methodical in her approach to assignments, which often results in high-quality work. Sydney Palmer understands concepts at an average pace and is punctual in starting her work and turning it in on time.

In terms of behavior, Sydney Palmer consistently follows rules and communicates effectively with the teacher, both rated as 'Far exceeds expectations.' She is generally accepted by her peers and is respectful towards others, both rated as 'Average.' Sydney Palmer's participation in class is also considered 'Average.'

Academic Performance

Sydney Palmer's academic abilities are rated as 'Average' in Language Arts, Writing, Classwork, and Homework. However, she is rated 'Below grade level expectations' in Test taking, which may be an area that requires additional support. Despite this, Sydney Palmer has shown remarkable improvement, as evidenced by her recent exam score of 71 out of 76.

Strengths and Weaknesses

Sydney Palmer's observed strengths include being hardworking, detail-oriented, and having good communication skills. She is also adept at self-advocacy. A noted weakness is that she takes longer than most to process information, but she compensates for this with her strong work ethic.

## Interventions and Support

Interventions that have been tried with Sydney Palmer include providing extra time on assignments and checking for understanding. These strategies appear to be effective, as there are no current concerns regarding her behavior or social skills. Sydney Palmer observes classroom expectations, is respectful to others, and has excellent attendance, always arriving on time.

Academic Summary from Melisa Whitcombe

Sydney Palmer's current grade in Education Pathways 1 for Quarter 4 is an A- with a score of 554 out of 612 (90.5%). Her performance in general classwork is exceptional, with a score of 294 out of 299 (98.3%, A+). She has scored a B in both Projects (163/197, 82.7%) and Assessments (97/116, 83.6%). Notably, Sydney Palmer has no missing assignments.

Sydney Palmer is described as a hardworking and conscientious student who demonstrates strong work habits and respectful behavior in the classroom. While she may require additional time to process information, her improvement and high-quality work reflect her dedication to her studies. Her academic performance is solid, with no current areas of concern.

**PE Teacher Input**

Malcolm Ferris, the PE 10 teacher, has shared his observations and insights regarding Sydney Palmer's performance and behavior in his class. While specific ratings on her work and academic abilities were not provided due to the nature of PE, his narrative offers a clear picture of Sydney Palmer's current situation.

Strengths and Weaknesses

Sydney Palmer is recognized for her respectful demeanor and her willingness to advocate for herself. She is proactive in seeking help or clarification when needed, which is a positive trait in her approach to learning and participation. However, she is noted to be quite shy, which seems to affect her interaction with peers and can lead to her feeling overwhelmed. In such instances, Sydney Palmer tends to seek solitude and visit the restroom, nurse or wellness center.

Behavior

In terms of her behavior, Sydney Palmer is punctual and arrives prepared for class, demonstrating respect towards both her teacher and her classmates. She adheres to class rules and participates in activities to the best of her ability. Her shyness, however, presents itself as a challenge, particularly in the context of group work, which is a significant component of the PE 10 curriculum.

## Interventions and Support

To support Sydney Palmer, Malcolm Ferris has implemented an intervention where he actively places her in groups where she feels more at ease. This strategy aims to alleviate the anxiety she experiences in team sports and group activities. While there has been some improvement, Malcolm Ferris expresses a desire to see Sydney Palmer become more comfortable in group settings, as this is an important skill for both her academic and real-world interactions.

Overall, Malcolm Ferris input highlights Sydney Palmer's strengths in self-advocacy and respectfulness, while also drawing attention to the areas where she could benefit from further support, particularly in overcoming her shyness and anxiety in group interactions. Sydney Palmer's academic standing in PE 10 is strong, with a current grade of "A-".

Sydney Palmer got close with one friend, but when all students returned to campus in 8th grade, that friend went back to her previous crowd, and that was really devastating for Sydney Palmer. As the 8th grade year went on, her social circle got smaller and smaller by her own choice, I think as a way to avoid getting hurt again and possibly to avoid difficult goodbyes, as she would not be going to the same high school as her peers. This was also by her own choice; Sydney Palmer was at a charter in Sacramento and wanted to go to the neighborhood school her brothers had attended for high school). By the end of eighth grade, she didn't have any friends, but was looking forward to a fresh start in high school. In the first week or so of summer between freshman and sophomore year, Sydney Palmer got sick with a stomach bug while her dad and I were out of town. She had already been suffering with anxiety and OCD, and an extreme fear of throwing up. That event, perhaps more than anything, let to a steep decline in her mental health. She was treated for avoidant restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) as a result, and stopped wanting to get in the car, for fear of getting carsick. She was in a very bad place, mentally, when freshman year started, and that is when the family really saw the effects of the social anxiety. Sydney Palmer had to take a leave from school (she did independent study) from late September through the beginning of January to do outpatient treatment at the Anxiety Treatment Center. When she returned to school in January, her social anxiety was as present as it had been before, although she was functioning slightly better in other ways. Sydney Palmer has been seeing this therapist for a year, was with another one for the year prior to that (that therapist moved), and before that, had a therapist with Kaiser. Mother indicates that her concerns, “have been that the school (the math teachers in particular, but also the IEP team) did not provide Sydney Palmer with a free and appropriate education in Integrated Math 2. She was not given appropriate accommodations, and the only help they offered was given outside the regular class time. We paid for private tutoring one or two times per weekly depending on whether there was a test. Sydney Palmer turned in almost all of her homework and class assignments, earning A in those areas, but she failed quizzes and tests. The onus was 100% on Sydney Palmer to pass the class, without sensitivity or consideration of her learning disability. The teachers were inflexible and admitted to not having experience in dyscalculia. Even the Education Specialist in her co-taught class did not take any responsibility for making the material more accessible for her. Sydney Palmer received an F for the first half of the course, which she made up before school with a general education teacher in the math department to a D- (that was part of an agreement that once Sydney Palmer hit a D, they would be finished). Sydney Palmer had to do this make-up while learning the material for the second half of the course simultaneously, which was just not feasible for her. She got an F for the second half as well. We pleaded for better accommodations or a modification to the weighting of the grading (it was something like 85% on tests, 10% quizzes, and 5% homework). We were told “no” over and over again by the IEP team. Mrs. Palmer states that, “The school told us the only way they would consider looking at making changes was if they did a brand new assessment, even though her triennial wasn't due until next year. We agreed (on the advice of our attorney), and what came out of that was that she no longer qualified as having a learning disability in math, and that it was her "emotional disturbance" that was causing her to perform so poorly in math. That led to the IEE request.”
**Therapist Input

** Rachel Simmons is Sydney Palmer’s private therapist. She provided the following input: 1. Challenges: What do you perceive as Sydney Palmer's most significant challenges in the school environment? “In my work with Sydney Palmer as her individual therapist, she and I have identified her social anxiety and OCD to be her biggest challenges at school. Some of her symptomatic expressions of social anxiety include distress in asking for support from or approaching teachers; she reports she will often not ask for help for fear of being perceived as dumb, or even to prevent feeling all eyes on her/being noticed by peers. Additionally, her OCD can create obstacles to her attendance to instruction in class if she has a compulsion to erase entire class notes due to one mistake, and then be unable to recreate the information nor attend to the current information being supplied.” 2.
**Effective Strategies:

** _Are there any strategies or support systems currently in place that you feel are working particularly well for her?_ “Ashely’s biggest support system comes from her parents, particularly her mom with whom she is very comfortable relating her struggles and asking for advice from. Sydney Palmer has not specifically identified interventions at school that have worked particularly well (though that may be due to our session focus being elsewhere).” 3.
**Impact of Math Difficulties:

** _How has her lack of success in math class affected her overall well-being and school experience?_ “Sydney Palmer struggles with self-esteem and her perception that others are thinking negatively about her. Her struggles in math compound the feelings of low self-worth, which impact other areas of school experiences. She reports little confidence with being able to become successful in math.” 4. Diagnoses and Recommendations: Based on your sessions with Sydney Palmer, do you have any diagnoses or recommendations that could inform the school’s approach to her education? “Sydney Palmer's Social Anxiety and OCD diagnoses seem to be impacting her school experiences and performance the most. Interventions with those in mind may be more successful. It is often that she may be limiting herself from asking for help from teachers or peers due to her Social Anxiety, particularly anxiety around how they may perceive her or if she's feeling especially anxious about having any attention paid to her. Sydney Palmer's OCD symptoms are primarily covert - the struggle is often invisible driven by obsessive thoughts and compulsions usually showing up as a 'need' to abort or avoid the task at hand, or perform a compulsion that impacts her ability to keep up (as in the need to erase the entirety of class notes to rectify one mistake). When she is experiencing OCD symptoms, her attention is greatly reduced elsewhere. Sydney Palmer has great desire to do well in school, both for her future and for her families' and her own expectations. She is very frustrated by the anxiety and OCD symptoms that can often impair her in being as successful as she wants to be.” 5. School's Role: In your view, how can the school further assist Sydney Palmer in her learning journey, especially in addressing her math-related challenges? “Exploration of any anxieties/intrusive thoughts that she may be experiencing, and the compulsions that may be associated with them could aid the interventionist's understanding of the role her diagnoses may or may not be playing in that particular learning experience.”
**Education Pathways
**Teacher Input

** Education Pathways teacher, Melisa Whitcombe, provided the following input of Sydney Palmer's performance and behavior in her class. ## Work Habits and Behavior Sydney Palmer is described as a diligent student who initiates work independently, scoring an 'Above Average' rating in this area. She is persistent in her efforts and does not give up easily. While her concentration and attentiveness are rated as 'Average,' she is methodical in her approach to assignments, which often results in high-quality work. Sydney Palmer understands concepts at an average pace and is punctual in starting her work and turning it in on time. In terms of behavior, Sydney Palmer consistently follows rules and communicates effectively with the teacher, both rated as 'Far exceeds expectations.' She is generally accepted by her peers and is respectful towards others, both rated as 'Average.' Sydney Palmer's participation in class is also considered 'Average.' Academic Performance Sydney Palmer's academic abilities are rated as 'Average' in Language Arts, Writing, Classwork, and Homework. However, she is rated 'Below grade level expectations' in Test taking, which may be an area that requires additional support. Despite this, Sydney Palmer has shown remarkable improvement, as evidenced by her recent exam score of 71 out of 76. Strengths and Weaknesses Sydney Palmer's observed strengths include being hardworking, detail-oriented, and having good communication skills. She is also adept at self-advocacy. A noted weakness is that she takes longer than most to process information, but she compensates for this with her strong work ethic. ## Interventions and Support Interventions that have been tried with Sydney Palmer include providing extra time on assignments and checking for understanding. These strategies appear to be effective, as there are no current concerns regarding her behavior or social skills. Sydney Palmer observes classroom expectations, is respectful to others, and has excellent attendance, always arriving on time. Academic Summary from Melisa Whitcombe Sydney Palmer's current grade in Education Pathways 1 for Quarter 4 is an A- with a score of 554 out of 612 (90.5%). Her performance in general classwork is exceptional, with a score of 294 out of 299 (98.3%, A+). She has scored a B in both Projects (163/197, 82.7%) and Assessments (97/116, 83.6%). Notably, Sydney Palmer has no missing assignments. Sydney Palmer is described as a hardworking and conscientious student who demonstrates strong work habits and respectful behavior in the classroom. While she may require additional time to process information, her improvement and high-quality work reflect her dedication to her studies. Her academic performance is solid, with no current areas of concern.

Malcolm Ferris, the PE 10 teacher, has shared his observations and insights regarding Sydney Palmer's performance and behavior in his class. While specific ratings on her work and academic abilities were not provided due to the nature of PE, his narrative offers a clear picture of Sydney Palmer's current situation. Strengths and Weaknesses Sydney Palmer is recognized for her respectful demeanor and her willingness to advocate for herself. She is proactive in seeking help or clarification when needed, which is a positive trait in her approach to learning and participation. However, she is noted to be quite shy, which seems to affect her interaction with peers and can lead to her feeling overwhelmed. In such instances, Sydney Palmer tends to seek solitude and visit the restroom, nurse or wellness center. Behavior In terms of her behavior, Sydney Palmer is punctual and arrives prepared for class, demonstrating respect towards both her teacher and her classmates. She adheres to class rules and participates in activities to the best of her ability. Her shyness, however, presents itself as a challenge, particularly in the context of group work, which is a significant component of the PE 10 curriculum. ## Interventions and Support To support Sydney Palmer, Malcolm Ferris has implemented an intervention where he actively places her in groups where she feels more at ease. This strategy aims to alleviate the anxiety she experiences in team sports and group activities. While there has been some improvement, Malcolm Ferris expresses a desire to see Sydney Palmer become more comfortable in group settings, as this is an important skill for both her academic and real-world interactions. Overall, Malcolm Ferris input highlights Sydney Palmer's strengths in self-advocacy and respectfulness, while also drawing attention to the areas where she could benefit from further support, particularly in overcoming her shyness and anxiety in group interactions. Sydney Palmer's academic standing in PE 10 is strong, with a current grade of "A-".

## **Overall Summary of Previous Evaluations and Academic History**

Jordan Ellis’s high school transcript (2023–2026) demonstrates ongoing academic progress in a range of core content areas. Since the 2022 psychoeducational evaluation, which documented significant deficits in mathematics and executive functioning, Jordan Ellis has successfully completed and is currently passing high school-level mathematics courses (Algebra I: B; Geometry: B, in progress). This represents a notable improvement from his prior performance on standardized achievement testing, where his math calculation and problem-solving skills were in the very low range. Jordan Ellis continues to perform at or above average in English/Language Arts and Science courses, consistent with previously identified strengths in reading and writing. His cumulative GPA is 3.02 (unweighted), with 8.5 credits earned, and he remains on track academically for his grade (but not necessarily his age), though additional credits are needed for graduation. There are no significant behavioral or disciplinary concerns noted. Jordan Ellis’s academic history reflects the positive impact of targeted interventions, accommodations, and a structured learning environment, though he continues to demonstrate needs in the areas of attention, executive functioning, and mathematics, warranting ongoing supports as previously recommended.

**PARENT INPUT**

Parent input was obtained through interview and review of recent health and available developmental history. Jordan Ellis currently resides with his adoptive parents, two younger sisters, and a younger brother. The family has experienced some transitions in recent years, including a move in 2020 and a parental job change in 2021. Jordan Ellis was adopted, and information regarding his early history, development and milestones is limited. It is reported that Jordan Ellis’s biological mother used substances, including drugs and alcohol, and experienced significant emotional stress during pregnancy. Details regarding pregnancy, labor, and delivery are otherwise unknown to this evaluator.

Jordan Ellis has a history of ADHD, diagnosed at his pediatrician’s office and confirmed via computerized assessment around age 10. He sustained a concussion in 2015 but is reported to have made a full recovery without lasting effects. Jordan Ellis was diagnosed with bipolar disorder by Dr. Aaron Whitfield in 2024. Current health is described as good, with no significant medical concerns or allergies. Jordan Ellis is a light sleeper but generally sleeps through the night. He has a reduced appetite in the morning, typically eating later in the day, and prefers foods high in sugar and carbohydrates. Vision screening (last completed through Medi-Cal) was within normal limits (20/20), and dental care is up to date, with cavities filled October 2025.

Jordan Ellis is currently prescribed Rexulti and Wellbutrin. Parent reports that Rexulti has stabilized his mood, reduced reactivity, and improved his ability to engage in meaningful conversations. Wellbutrin is perceived to provide some increase in motivation, particularly for activities of interest, but has not sufficiently improved his motivation for schoolwork. Jordan Ellis himself does not perceive significant benefit from his medication.

Jordan Ellis’s routine includes attending church on Sundays, where he volunteers in the toddler room. He maintains a part-time work schedule of approximately 20 hours a week at Ground Control Suspension, independently waking and preparing for his shifts, with some flexibility provided by his employer. Social interactions include weekly gatherings with family friends, providing opportunities for engagement with both adults and younger children. Jordan Ellis enjoys video games and playing the drums. He also loves basketball, with practices continuing outside of the season; however, participation is contingent upon completion of schoolwork.

Jordan Ellis’s primary household responsibilities include schoolwork and emptying the dishwasher. He is described as charming, good with young children, and a hard worker when supervised. Parent concerns include volatility and intimidation toward siblings, a strong need for control, and difficulty accepting guidance or correction. Jordan Ellis’s relationships with siblings are variable, and while he generally gets along with peers, he does not maintain ongoing contact with them.

Interventions to date have included an IEP, vision therapy, tutoring, Internal Family Systems therapy, internal listening system, LENS neurofeedback, talk therapy, and counseling. Parent reports ongoing concerns with attention, distractibility, poor focus, impulsivity, disorganization, difficulty following directions, and challenges with task initiation and completion. Jordan Ellis has attended multiple schools and has experienced academic struggles throughout, with the COVID-19 pandemic and distance learning exacerbating his difficulties. He initially attended Ponderosa High School but began experimenting with drugs, was involved in physical altercations on campus, and engaged in aggressive behavior at home, prompting a transition to online schooling.

The parent’s primary goals for this assessment are to better understand the underlying causes of Jordan Ellis’s behavioral and academic challenges, clarify the presence of any mental health, behavioral, or developmental issues, and receive recommendations for treatment and support to facilitate a successful transition to adulthood.
